President Paul Kagame’s first-ever state visit to Cambodia has opened a new chapter in relations between the two countries.

It featured a royal reception, a state banquet hosted by King Norodom Sihamoni and the signing of three bilateral agreements.

Kagame arrived in Phnom Penh on November 12. He was accompanied by First Lady Mrs Jeannette Kagame and a high-level delegation. The visit is the first by a Rwandan Head of State to the Southeast Asian kingdom.

On Friday, November 13, Kagame held bilateral talks with Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet at the Peace Palace. They discussed ways to expand economic cooperation, strengthen trade and investment ties, and increase collaboration in tourism and aviation.

The two leaders witnessed the exchange of three agreements.

The first was a memorandum of understanding between the Rwanda Development Board (RDB) and Cambodia’s Council for the Development of Cambodia (CDC). It aims to promote investment and strengthen cooperation between the two institutions.

The agreement provides for the exchange of experience and investment opportunities. It also seeks to build closer links between businesses in both countries.

The second agreement established a framework for tourism cooperation. It provides for joint promotion and exchanges between relevant institutions.

The third was a Bilateral Air Services Agreement. It creates a framework for aviation cooperation and could support future air connections between the two countries. However, no direct flights between Kigali and Phnom Penh have been announced.

During the talks, Hun Manet welcomed Kagame and the Rwandan delegation. Kagame, in turn, commended Cambodia’s recovery and socio-economic progress after the devastation of the Khmer Rouge era.

President Kagame said the two countries could use their complementary positions to expand trade.

Rwanda could serve as a gateway to African markets for Cambodian businesses. Cambodia, meanwhile, could provide Rwandan companies with access to Southeast Asian markets.

The leaders also discussed cooperation in other sectors. They addressed transnational crime, including technology-enabled scams.

They also exchanged views on cooperation through international platforms. These include the United Nations, the Non-Aligned Movement and the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie.

Kagame also met Senate President Hun Sen. They discussed the two countries’ shared experiences of national tragedy, recovery and rebuilding.

Both sides emphasised resilience and self-reliance. They also highlighted the importance of stronger bilateral relations.

Another meeting brought Kagame together with National Assembly President Khuon Sudary. Their discussions covered parliamentary cooperation and bilateral relations.

They also addressed gender equality and women’s representation in leadership.

The diplomatic engagements were accompanied by formal ceremonies that reflected the importance Cambodia attached to the visit.

At the Royal Palace, King Norodom Sihamoni received Kagame and the First Lady with full state honours. The King later granted them a royal audience.

Kagame also laid wreaths at the Independence Monument. He paid tribute at the memorial dedicated to the late King-Father Norodom Sihanouk.

The visit’s highlight came on Friday evening. King Norodom Sihamoni hosted a state banquet in honour of Kagame, the First Lady and the Rwandan delegation.

The banquet brought together senior Cambodian leaders. They included Hun Sen, Khuon Sudary and Hun Manet, who was accompanied by his spouse, Pich Chanmony.

Both leaders spoke. In his remarks, Kagame described the visit as the beginning of a stronger partnership between the two countries.

“Rwanda is very happy to be working with Cambodia,” he said. “From the productive discussions we have had today, it is evident that our aspirations are closely aligned. This visit is the beginning of a new chapter, that will strengthen our cooperation, and bonds of friendship.”

He said both countries were keen to diversify their economies and accelerate development through investment.

Rwanda, he added, looked forward to learning from Cambodia’s experience.

“Together, we are interested in diversifying our economies, and accelerating development through investment. Cambodia is emerging as one of the fastest-growing markets in the region, and we look forward to continuing to learn from your experience,” Kagame said.

The visit comes as Cambodia prepares to host the 20th Summit of La Francophonie from November 14 to 16. The summit will be held under the theme “Reinvesting in Peace for Shared Prosperity and Lasting Stability”.

Rwanda and Cambodia established diplomatic relations in 2005. Their cooperation has since included agreements on bilateral consultations and visa exemptions for holders of diplomatic and official passports.

Both were signed in 2025. The two countries have also pursued earlier financial cooperation initiatives.

The three agreements signed during Kagame’s visit provide a further basis for expanding relations, particularly in investment, tourism and aviation.

Brazil great Ronaldinho is set to make his first competitive start in more than a decade when Ravenna face local rivals Forli in Italy's third division on Sunday.

The former Barcelona and AC Milan playmaker, 46, is in line to make his first appearance for Ravenna since joining the Serie C club in August .

His last competitive appearance came for Brazilian side Fluminense in September 2015 .

Ravenna manager Andrea Mandorlini said on Friday that Ronaldinho would start the match as one of his side's three forwards.

Former Ballon d'Or winner Ronaldinho initially joined the Italian club as an investor in August, but said he had ambitions of scoring one final goal to take his career tally to 300.

"His objective is romantic, to try to score his last goal," club owner Ignazio Cipriani said earlier this year.

"His involvement is not a token gesture or a marketing stunt to get people talking about us."

The Brazilian arrived in Italy on Friday and will have only one training session with his team-mates before Sunday's match.

A temporary stand has been created at Ravenna's Stadio Bruno Benelli to accommodate the expected crowd, with supporters hoping to catch a glimpse of the World Cup winner in action for potentially the final time.

On Saturday, the biggest and longest-running international song contest will make a leap into unknown territory.

Eurovision, the pan-European competition famed for zany gimmicks, slick, sometimes over-the-top staging, the drama of its complex voting system and, occasionally, for outstanding music, celebrates its 70th birthday this year.

And to mark it, the European Broadcasting Union is trying out audiences in Asia.

It's an idea that's been talked about for two decades but never materialised, despite many false starts.

Until now - Eurovision Asia will hold its first grand final in Bangkok, starting at 20:30 ICT (13:30 GMT).

Transferring one of the most successful television formulas that has worked in Europe for 70 years to Asia has not been straightforward, says Sarun 'Note' Kungbunpot, a Eurovision enthusiast and Thai singer who has won several competitions in this region.

"It's still very new in Asia. I'm not sure many people have heard about it yet," he says, adding that he thinks it will take a bit of time for audiences to adjust.

"When we look at contests in Thailand, the Philippines and Korea, we actually compete based on the singer.

"It's all about popularity – fans are looking for their idols. But Eurovision is all about the song, not the singer. I think this needs to be communicated clearly."

MANG x DAOU have winning form, having previously been declared champions of the show Thailand's Chosen One

Then there is the long history of Eurovision in Europe. It began in 1956 as a project to encourage greater cultural exchanges in a Europe which was trying to forge a common future after two world wars.

This was the very start of the age of mass television ownership, and Eurovision became such a fixture it is now an indelible piece of Europe's shared cultural heritage. It has no such resonance in Asia, and arrives in this region in the digital age, when traditional TV formats are struggling to cut through.

Only 11 countries are taking part in this first Eurovision Asia contest – host Thailand, along with Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, South Korea, Mongolia, Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan.

Asian giants India, China, Japan and Indonesia are noticeably absent, although there are negotiations ongoing to try to get them into next year's contest, assuming there is one.

There have also been problems with the organisation of this event.

A sudden million-dollar (£760,000) budget cut just three weeks before the final meant many of the technicians familiar with staging Eurovision were not brought to Thailand, and there have been a number of staff resignations too.

Eurovision fans - and there are many passionate followers around the world - have noticed, criticising audio and lighting in rehearsal videos.

Watch: Eurovision is coming to Asia - but will it succeed?

The contest's unusual voting system will be unfamiliar to Asian audiences. Like in Europe, Eurovision Asia will determine the winner through a 50/50 mix of public voting and national juries from each of the 11 contesting countries, as well as a 12th "rest of the world" category.

Anyone can vote - you get eight votes once you register - but you cannot vote for your own country's contestant and you must give your votes to at least three others.

The public and jury votes are then converted into points. The most popular song among the Bhutanese or Mongolians, for example, will get 12 points from those countries, while the song ranked last will get zero - the famous "nul points".

JUNHEE is a solo singer-songwriter from South Korea who produces bright, mainstream-sounding music

In Europe, there have long been reports of co-ordinated voting to back neighbours, for example the four Nordic countries voting for each other. This seems less likely in Eurovision Asia, but political differences, for example between Thailand and Cambodia after their border war last year, could influence how their audiences vote.

Filipinos, with their passion for singing, are expected to be enthusiastic participants and the 11 million who live overseas might make a difference. But as most live and work in countries which are not participating, their votes will only go into the "rest of the world" pool.

For Bhutan, with a population of less than a million, this is a rare chance to shine on a global stage, which puts some pressure on 24-year-old Thukten Nyendra, the singer representing the Himalayan kingdom in Bangkok with his song Lhayi Semo (The Angel). Before coming here he had never left his country or been on a plane before.

"I'm not a star. I'm just Nyendra over there," he told the BBC. "Nobody knows me. But Eurovision has given me a huge platform. Actually winning would mean the world to us... If I really make it through all of this, it would mean the entire freaking world to us."

Nyendra, Bhutan's 24-year-old contestant, is also a journalism graduate

The other characteristic of Eurovision is the song format – no more than three minutes, no more than six people on stage, and no backing band, only taped music.

This encourages performers to prepare elaborate, sometimes outrageous choreography and stunts to impress the audience – think Poland's My Słowianie in 2014 with models in traditional costume churning butter on stage, or the Finnish heavy metal band Lordi donning flamboyant monster outfits in its 2006 entry.

There has also been a long association of Eurovision with LGBTQ+ artists. Eurovision Asia includes Malaysia and Bangladesh – where same-sex activity is illegal – and there are no visible LGBTQ+ elements this year.

Performers have been using the last days of rehearsals before the final to try to make their stage acts as striking as possible. Thinla from Laos has abandoned the short, sequinned dress she wore in the first video of her infectious reggaeton song Bae and is adopting Lao hill-tribe costume for her and her backing dancers.

Thinla's music blends traditional Lao and contemporary genres, such as pop, R&B and dance

Perhaps the most ambitious choreography is in Vietnamese singer Tóc Tiên's song Em Tiên ("Fairy Maiden").

It has been exhausting just watching her rehearse the elaborate moves and costume changes for more than an hour at a time.

The entry from Bangladesh's Beatmosphere, Tumi Ele ("You Came"), is unusual as an a cappella and beatboxing performance by six men with little backing music.

The youngest contestant is 19 year-old Carmelle Collado from the Philippines, whose bubbling confidence and strong stage presence in her song Sobra-Sobra ("Too Much") belie her youth.

"I'm actually quite scared because I'm the youngest, but also really happy," she told us.

"The song is about feminine energy. It's about being brave, strong, fierce, and it's about how strong Filipino women are."

Bangladesh's Beatmosphere blend traditional vocal harmony with beatbox culture

Carmelle Collado rose to prominence through a selection of televised singing competitions in the Philippines

Eurovision is famous for putting unknown acts onto a global stage, and introducing musicians who went on to become megastars – think Abba, little known when they won in 1974 with Waterloo, and Celine Dion winning in Ireland in 1988.

Because of the lack of public awareness of Eurovision Asia many of the finalists chosen for this first contest are already well known in their home markets.

Aina Abdul is perhaps the most famous singer in Malaysia, known as much for dramatic costumes as her impressive vocal range. Her song Bluest Sky – which she told us was inspired by her late cat Hiro – is a strong contender to win the contest.

Malaysia's Aina Abdul laughs as designer Melinda Looi adjusts her dress before a media shoot

Abdul's spectacular dress, by Malaysian designer Melinda Looi, who has travelled to Bangkok with her, had taken 600 hours to make, she told me. She said its glistening texture, made from materials brought from Italy and China, is meant to represent moving water.

If all goes well on the night, the organisers are hoping this could be the start of an expansion of the hugely successful Eurovision brand into a region which, after all, has half the world's population.

Montreal, Canada was badly hit by the Great Ice Storm of 1998 which was blamed, in part, on El Niño.

The developing El Niño - already the strongest on record by some measures - continues to grow and could have profound effects on the weather across North America this autumn and winter.

The naturally-occurring climate phenomenon sees trade winds over the Pacific Ocean, which usually blow from east to west, weakening or reversing with warm water instead spreading eastwards.

This releases heat into the atmosphere which can drive major shifts in global weather patterns.

Impacts in the US and Canada are varied, with a greater chance of a warm and dry winter in northern areas and more risk of flooding rain further south.

There is also some evidence that El Niño can increase the likelihood of disruption to the stratospheric polar vortex which can, in turn, bring snowfall later in winter.

No two El Niños are the same and the impacts are not guaranteed - the odds are just shifted in favour of certain outcomes.

UN warns of 'supersized' El Niño as countries prepare for impact

The eastward shift of warm ocean waters associated with El Niño can cause the Pacific jet stream to move south and extend eastwards, directing rain-bearing weather systems across the southern USA.

This typically leads to wetter winters during El Niño years.

The likely impacts of El Niño on winter weather vary across different parts of North America.

The latest three month forecast , external from the US National Weather Service (NWS) suggests this is a likely outcome for the winter of 2026-2027.

South-eastern states, including Florida, Georgia and the Carolinas, have the greatest chance of seeing above-average rainfall.

The El Niño winter of 1997-1998 brought significant flooding in the south-east and spun up tornadoes for Florida.

Severe flooding hit Long Beach, California in February 2024.

California could well find itself in the firing line with forecasts suggesting a wet winter is likely.

Governor Gavin Newsom has already declared a state of emergency , external ahead of anticipated floods and mudslides.

Areas scarred by recent wildfires are particularly susceptible, with the effects of climate change exacerbating the risks.

Many past El Niños have been wet here, with winter 2023-2024 bringing relief from drought. However this is not always the case. In the strong El Niño of 2015-2016, California actually had below-average rainfall.

Coastal erosion and large waves could be worsened by a rise in the overall sea level driven by so-called Kelvin waves.

This is where ocean water which sloshes eastwards across the Pacific due to El Niño reaches the west coast of the Americas, where it can travel no further.

It causes a large-scale wave which then spreads along the coast over a period of weeks and months, raising sea levels by 15cm (6in) or more.

The shift of the Pacific jet stream generally leads to warmer and milder winters in the north-west USA, Northern Plains and Ohio Valley - as well as western and central Canada.

This lessens the risk of flooding, but reduced rainfall can leave groundwater and river levels low, fuelling drought and wildfires in spring and summer.

Ski resorts can also suffer from a lack of snow.

Long-range predictions suggest a dry, warm winter is more likely than usual this year.

However, El Niño does not guarantee this. For instance, the winters of 1982-1983 and 2015-2016 were wetter than normal in the north-west USA.

In much of the northern USA, and large swathes of Canada, a greater chance of dry and warm weather makes snow less likely.

Further south, however, above-average precipitation typically leads to big snowfalls in the Californian mountains and southern Rockies - good news for water stocks.

It can also increase the probability of snow at lower levels in the southern and eastern USA - but only if enough cold air is in the mix.

The area around Washington DC often receives more snowfall than usual in an El Niño winter - but not always.

Snowfall caused chaos in Washington DC in February 2010.

The winter of 2009-2010 delivered record-breaking snowfall that brought the city to a standstill, while widespread blizzards affected much of the US east coast in 2016.

However, some of Washington DC's least snowy winters have also occurred during El Niño events, including 1972-1973 and 1997-1998 which brought just 0.1in (0.25cm) of snow.

Higher winter temperatures in eastern Canada and the north-east USA can mean precipitation that might normally fall as snow gives rain instead.

This can increase the chance of freezing rain events, with the so-called Great Ice Storm of 1998 , external being blamed partly on the effects of El Niño.

It is worth saying that snowfall amounts are decreasing overall in most places due to human-induced climate change, meaning predicting the impact of El Niño is even more complex.

An added complication is the possible impact of El Niño on the polar vortex, a ring of strong winds that circles the North Pole in winter, around 10-30 miles (16-48km) up in the stratosphere.

It holds cold, dense air in place above the Arctic but sometimes it can weaken and disrupt, and there is some evidence that the energy released into the atmosphere by El Niño makes this more likely.

Disruptions to the polar vortex sometimes ripple down through the atmosphere, weakening the polar jet stream and opening the door for cold air to spill across Canada and the USA.

However this does not always occur and the links are far from clear.

Tolu Arokodare has scored 13 goals in 17 appearances this season after joining Ajax on loan from Wolves

Tolu Arokodare was the hero as Nigeria boosted their hopes of reaching the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) with a 3-1 home win over tournament co-hosts Tanzania.

With the East Africans already assured of a spot at the finals, the Super Eagles are battling for the one qualification spot available in Group L and have little margin for error after losing 3-0 in Guinea-Bissau in September.

Alhassan Yusuf kept his composure to slot Nigeria into a second-minute lead in Uyo from Ademola Lookman's pass, but the visitors equalised through Alphonce Msanga just after the half-hour mark.

Arokodare climbed off the bench at half-time and cleverly flicked home Wilfred Ndidi's low ball to restore the lead for the West Africans in the 52nd minute.

And the Ajax striker, who is on a season-long loan from Wolves, gave the Super Eagles breathing space eight minutes later when he controlled Moses Usor's cross from the left and smashed in from 12 yards out.

With three games played in the group, Eric Chelle's side are now one point behind leaders Guinea-Bissau, who drew 1-1 with Madagascar on Thursday.

Ghana kick-start Afcon 2027 bid despite Ayew penalty miss

Why has Caf abandoned plans to hold Afcon every four years?

Elsewhere, Mohamed Salah scored twice late on against Malawi as Egypt cruised to a 5-0 victory in Ali Maher's first match in charge.

Achraf Hakimi netted two stunning goals and Yassine Bounou saved a penalty to help Morocco continue their unbeaten start with a 5-1 win over Niger.

Meanwhile, Tunisia are in danger of missing out on the finals for the first time since 1992 after suffering a 2-0 defeat at home against Libya, and Kenya scored a last-minute equaliser to end South Africa's perfect start.

The third round of qualifying culminates with three games on Saturday, while the fourth round of fixtures are split across Monday and Tuesday.

The most recent of Egypt's record seven Afcon titles came in 2010, and Mohamed Salah (right) has finished as a runner-up twice with the Pharaohs since then

Egypt reached the semi-finals of Afcon 2025 and the last 16 of this year's Fifa World Cup under Hossam Hassan but parted company with the 60-year-old earlier this month.

The Pharaohs had taken four points from their opening two games in Group B, with Salah substituted after an hour in their 0-0 draw with Angola before missing the win in South Sudan.

The former Liverpool forward returned as captain against Malawi, and Egypt cruised into a 3-0 lead at the break through goals from Nasser Maher, Omar Marmoush and Mohamed Hany.

Salah got on the scoresheet when he stooped to head in a cross from the left and rounded off proceedings by dinking in a penalty after Hamza Abdelkarim was tripped in the box.

Victory in Maher's first game at the helm puts Egypt three points clear of Angola, who take on South Sudan on Saturday.

In Group A, Morocco had also looked like they would ease to three points against Niger in Casablanca after Yassir Zabiri's early effort and a brilliant long-range strike from right-back Hakimi put them 2-0 up after 27 minutes.

But Mohamed Abdourahmane headed in to halve the deficit and Niger had a chance to level from the spot on the stroke of half-time after a handball by Noussair Mazraoui.

However, Atlas Lions goalkeeper Bounou moved to his left to keep out Youssouf Oumarou's penalty, and Hakimi made it 3-1 in first-half stoppage time with a dipping free-kick from distance.

Youssef En-Nesyri steered in the fourth in the 77th minute from a Hakimi pass and Ayoub Oufkir completed the scoring from close range in the final minute.

Earlier in Group A on Friday Gabon beat Lesotho to move on to six points thanks to two second-half goals from Denis Bouanga.

The LA FC forward smashed the right-hand upright with a penalty but broke the deadlock with a header a minute later and then scored from 12 yards when the Panthers were awarded a second spot kick.

Former South Africa international Benni McCarthy denied Bafana Bafana victory as his Kenya side grabbed a late equaliser

Tunisia have appeared at a record 17 consecutive Afcons but are winless and bottom of Group H - another section with just one qualifying place on offer - after defeat by their North African neighbours Libya.

The Carthage Eagles could complain about refereeing decisions going against them in Sfax, with Ali Maaloul penalised for a shirt pull on Muad Eisay just before half-time and Ali Youssef converting the resulting spot-kick.

Tunisia had a goal ruled out following a marginal offside call in the second half and three minutes later a low shot from Hamdou El Houni made it 2-0 to the Mediterranean Knights.

Libya, who last played at an Afcon in 2012, climb to second in the table and go level on points with Uganda.

South Africa are a point clear of Guinea at the top of Group D after a 2-2 draw against Benni McCarthy's Kenya in Johannesburg.

Amos Wanjala's own goal gifted the hosts an early lead before Michael Olunga levelled from the penalty spot just before half-time.

Relebohile Mofokeng restored Bafana Bafana's advantage with 13 minutes remaining, but Kenya claimed a point when Ryan Ogam's low shot from 20 yards crept inside the left-hand upright in the 90th minute.

Elsewhere, Burkina Faso joined Benin on seven points at the top of Group F thanks to Elohim Kabore's 94th-minute winner against Mauritania in Ouagadougou.

Mali extended their winning start to go top of Group K after Mamadou Camara completed a 3-2 comeback win at home against Rwanda, who had led twice in Bamako.

Rwanda had won their first two fixtures and are three points ahead of Cape Verde , who registered their first points with a 4-2 victory over Liberia in Praia.

Ethiopia registered their first win to upset Mozambique in Maputo, with Kenean Markneh scoring the only goal in the 87th minute after Mambas keeper Ernan spilled a low shot from Carlos Damtew.

The East Africans move on to three points but remain bottom of Group J, behind Sudan on head-to-head record, while Mozambique are on four points and three behind leaders Senegal.

Zambia moved level on four points with Group I leaders Algeria after a 1-1 draw at home to Burundi. The North Africans have the chance to open up a three-point gap when they host Togo on Saturday.

In Group G, Comoros were held to a goalless draw by Congo-Brazzaville in Moroni. Cameroon lead the section on seven points, with Comoros on four, Namibia on three and the Congolese bottom on two points.

The Pope, who has Peruvian citizenship, lived in Chiclayo for several years

Pope Leo XIV has celebrated Mass near the Peruvian city where he made his name as a compassionate bishop who worked closely with poor and migrant communities.

The ceremony was held on Friday at a park in Pimentel, about 10km (six miles) from Chiclayo in northern Peru as part of his tour of Latin America.

The Vatican estimates more than 1.5 million people gathered to welcome the pontiff.

"Thank you for your affection, support and prayers," the Pope told followers.

"Especially for my health during this time of trial which, with God's help, I am overcoming," he added, referencing the surgery he had for lung cancer which took place just weeks ago .

Some of the crowd arrived 12 hours in advance to wait in vigil before the Mass began.

"We spent the night praying, alongside family, excited to welcome the Pope from Chiclayo," said Isa Orderique.

Pope Leo celebrated Mass in front of a jubilant crowd

Many came from across Peru and even neighbouring countries to attend.

Merli Cruz Guerrero, from an area near the Ecuadorean border, travelled several hours by bus to attend. She also spent the entire night waiting.

Of all the events the Pope has attended so far during his visit to Peru, this felt particularly emotional.

The crowd fell into a hushed silence as the pontiff's motorcade approached.

They waited eagerly for his arrival despite spending long hours out in the open with the temperature pushing past 30C.

For many living here, the fact that the Pope worked extensively in this region before becoming the head of the Catholic Church has put them in the spotlight.

"The Pope has come home and Chiclayo is celebrating," said Lisbeth Díaz, a teacher who worked with Pope Leo when he served as the city's bishop between 2015 and 2023.

Lisbeth Díaz says Chiclayo is celebrating the Pope's return

Peru is the longest stop on the first tour of Latin America by the pontiff , who was elected in May 2025.

The trip has also taken in Argentina and Uruguay, but his time in this country carries particular significance.

The Pope not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.

Around Chiclayo, it is hard to meet anyone who doesn't claim to be a friend of the Pope or have a special anecdote about him.

Some recall how he would enjoy sampling Peruvian delicacies at El Trébol, a restaurant next to the city's cathedral. Others remember his love of tennis.

But for many it's the more serious moments of his time here, such as helping launch soup kitchens during the Covid-19 pandemic, or wading through deep waters on horseback when floods hit the area.

Several of these images are on display in a small museum dedicated to him at the entrance to the bishop's residence.

Commemorative pictures of the Pope are sold in the main of square of Chiclayo, including a famous image of him visiting a remote village on horseback

But for the city, and for a country that calls him the "Peruvian Pope", his return home means much more than a collection of photographs and anecdotes.

"It is the return of the man who brought Peruvians closer to the Church," said Samuel David Miranda Atoche, a local parish priest from Chiclayo who was ordained by the Pope back when he was still the bishop and known under his birth name of Robert Prevost.

And it is not just local people he connected with, according to Díaz, who came to Chiclayo from Venezuela.

"It was difficult for him to see so many migrants living on the streets," she added, recalling the time when large numbers of Venezuelans came through Chiclayo escaping the political and economic crisis in their home country.

"So, he got in touch with the migration authorities and coordinated with other organisations to speed up the paperwork needed for many of us to obtain legal residency and work permits."

Who is Robert Prevost, the new Pope Leo XIV?

Robert Prevost's time here as bishop also involved difficult decisions, such as having to deal with the controversy and scandal surrounding the dissolution of Sodalitium of Christian Life, a Peruvian Catholic organisation that had faced decades of sexual abuse allegations.

Santiago Roncagliolo, a Peruvian writer and journalist who has studied the Pope's life, believes his handling of that crisis earned him the favour of his predecessor, Pope Francis, and helped set him on the path to the papacy.

Father Miranda also stressed the role the now-pontiff played in bringing people together.

"If there is one thing Bishop Prevost worked for here," he added, referring to the Pope by his previous title, "it was unity".

That unity has been on display in the run up to the Mass, with the square in front of Chiclayo Cathedral filled with joyous celebrations for days.

Father Samuel David Miranda Atoche says the Pope brought Peruvians closer to the Church

Normally, 800,000 people live in the city and its surrounding area, but estimates say the Pope's visit has caused that to double.

Local businesses have been capitalising on the Pope's popularity to boost sales and hotels have sharply increased their nightly room rates.

But that didn't seem to put off the faithful who gathered for the Mass.

Shouts of: "The Pope is from Chiclayo!" echoed across the field during the event.

Their affection was clearly reflected by the pontiff.

"As I look at your faces, a prayer of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart," he said from the stage, "for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life."

The English Football League (EFL) has warned its members about their usage of posts on social media that might target other sides regarding disciplinary issues.

In September, Wrexham aimed a Spygate -based dig at Southampton in a video that featured their owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney in a cheeky social media post.

This came before the Dragons played Saints, eventually winning the Championship game 2-1 at the Racecourse Ground.

Wrexham's owners appeared on Wrexham's X account, which started with Reynolds emerging from behind a tree.

In a skit nominally aimed at promoting shirt sponsor Firefox, the Deadpool star said: "Today, for no particular reason, we want to talk about the importance of privacy."

A few weeks later, Southampton fired back at Wrexham after the Welsh club had been fined by the EFL for fielding two ineligible players.

Saints commented "hope you've double checked this one lads" on their X account under Wrexham's team news post for a following game against Sheffield United.

Birmingham City also joined in with the Spygate themed posts, with a graphic of both clubs' badges cut into grass hedges, shown through the eye of binoculars before playing each other in September.

The EFL has since sent a letter to club chairs and executives, advising clubs to avoid posts that could have a reputational impact.

MN202611_fnho83dnlt.t:
Boyhood Walsall fan Leigh Pomlett first joined the Saddlers board in 2010

Walsall co-chairman Leigh Pomlett has given a powerful response to the independent State of the Game report by suggesting some clubs "beggar belief" in the way they operate.

The revelation of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) in its first report that 94% of clubs made losses in the 2025-26 season suggested the majority of clubs were living "on the edge of financial disaster".

Pomlett told BBC Radio WM at a Walsall fans' forum at Bescot Stadium just how serious football's financial problems are. And, although he stressed that the Saddlers are better run than most, the League Two promotion contenders will still have to make significant cuts in spending to qualify for an IFR operating licence in future.

"The State of the Game report came out a couple of weeks ago," he said. "A report that has come out from the independent regulator. It is a huge report and I have, for my sins, read all 260 pages of it.

"It goes into huge detail and, for the first time ever, is about the state of English football, right from the Premier League to the National League.

"Football is in a shocking state. Some clubs would still lose money even if they paid their players nothing. That is a fact. Some clubs will have to radically change what they do."

Majority of clubs on edge of 'financial disaster' - regulator

"Compared to some clubs, we at Walsall are in a very good state of health but it's still tough - just a lot less tough than it will be for some other clubs in the EFL who just beggar belief.

"We are at times accused of lack of ambition for not being able to buy this or that player, but the priority is still to make the club sustainable."

In a week when fellow Midlands-based League Two club Shrewsbury Town were taken over by new American owners , Pomlett warns that the scope for any club looking to speculate to accumulate will have to be drastically toned down if the regulator deduces they are spending money they have not got.

"The losses from the top to the bottom are massive," said Pomlett.

"Clubs who are losing an absolute fortune every week will not be allowed to continue like that. 33 clubs do not have enough cash to survive a month. That's incredible.

Walsall co-chairman and former owner Leigh Pomlett (left), current chief executive Ben Sadler (centre) and former CEO Stefan Gamble, now club owners Trivela Group's head of finance, were part of the panel at the Saddlers' latest Fans Forum

"The losses being made in League One, League Two and the National League are enormous, but some of the Premier League and Championship losses are mind-boggling.

"The regulator is not going to let us carry on like that.

"We have to make sure this club remains solvent. Firstly because that is the right thing to do and secondly because there is now an independent financial regulator who will make sure that we do. We have to batten down the hatches in terms of costs.

"Profitablity will have to return to the days gone by. The purpose of the regulator being created was to never allow another Macclesfield.

"They now watch every club. The distribution of wealth will change. There is too much at the top and not enough further down.

"We're on the brink of the biggest change in the football industry that we've seen since the Premier League was first formed."

Catherine Zeta Jones moved to California in the 1990s to pursue an acting career

Catherine Zeta-Jones has said she had an ego check after moving to America in the 1990s.

The Swansea-born star had become a household name in the UK, but Hollywood quickly provided a reality check for the rising star and she was even asked by casting agents if she had any acting experience.

It was during her stint on CBS mini-series Titanic that she was seen by Steven Spielberg who suggested she go for a role in The Mask of Zorro, which he was producing.

"Five days later I got the job, and three days after that, I was down there starting my sword-fighting lessons," she said.

Zeta-Jones had become a star in the UK thanks to her breakout role in The Darling Buds of May that originally aired from 1991 to 1993.

But when she touched down in California, she was no longer recognised by the public and had a six-month visa to "give America a shot".

She told Business Insider , external it was "good" for her to have her ego knocked down a bit.

It was only when the Spielberg saw the Titanic series that she was given a major opportunity.

"I was shipped down to Mexico to screen test with Antonio Banderas," she said.

Catherine Zeta-Jones and Antonio Banderas at a premiere for The Mask of Zorro in 1998

She credits it as her breakthrough into A-list territory and it was rumoured that she beat actors such as Salma Hayek and Jennifer Lopez to the part.

Zeta-Jones went on to work with Sean Connery in Entrapment which cemented her stardom, and she refers to the late James Bond actor as a "dear force of nature".

"I just never wanted to stop acting with him, because we were such good buddies," she said.

"He was so incredibly protective of me, like a daughter he never had, and he said that to me."

Zeta-Jones says it has been "liberating" to use her Welsh accent in Kill Jackie

Zeta-Jones is currently starring in Kill Jackie, a revenge thriller based on the 2018 novel The Price You Pay by Nick Harkaway.

She stars as the titular Jackie Price, a Welsh high-end art dealer with a shady past in the drug trade who discovers a hit has been put out on her.

In September, Zeta-Jones made headlines for revealing that it was the first time she had used her Swansea accent for a role.

After decades of working on accents including English, American and Scottish she said the opportunity to speak in her native accent was both "liberating and cathartic".

As well as returning to her Welsh roots, the series' ultra-violent scenes have been a blast for Zeta-Jones, who relished the chance to go off the rails.

"I wanted the audience to come along on this ride with me and root for her. In all the craziness."

Estonia has become the latest country to say it will not allow Russian or Belarusian athletes to compete on its territory as a result of the ongoing war in Ukraine.

It comes after Norway, Finland and Canada made similar announcements.

The moves come amid a mounting backlash over the reinstatement of athletes from Russia and Belarus.

In September, the International Ski Federation (FIS) relaxed its rules, saying competitors from the two countries would be granted access to its events "provided that they sign a declaration of neutrality".

They had previously faced more stringent background checks on any voluntary link or paid duty with the military.

Participation remains limited to individual events, with athletes banned from displaying national symbols such as flags, anthems or uniforms.

However, it has now emerged that Estonia's government has written to the FIS, claiming that allowing entry to competitors from Russia and Belarus would undermine the country's support of Ukraine, and present an opportunity for propaganda. It said a ban issued in 2022 will be maintained.

In a statement issued to BBC Sport, the FIS said it "is committed to offering full support to athletes, national ski associations and local organisers - with most of which we have a long-standing relationship - in the process of navigating what we know to be a very complex situation.

"With that said, the Individual Neutral Athlete policy is clear in stating that notwithstanding eligibility, the host country visa and entry policies remain in place and are determined solely by the host country. FIS bears no responsibility for denial of visas or entry to any person granted eligibility under the FIS Individual Neutral Athlete Policy."

On Thursday, Scandinavian neighbours Norway and Finland both said they would also block visas for Russian athletes because of the war in Ukraine.

Norway is preparing to host the cross-country skiing World Cup next month, while Finland is due to stage the figure skating world championships in March. The International Skating Union (ISU) has said it "believes that athletes should not be punished for the actions of their governments in a world where, sadly, many conflicts are ongoing", and that it was "seeking clarifications" from officials in Finland.

This comes in the wake of last month's decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) to overturn a ban of Russia by the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), a move condemned by the British, German, Finnish and Czech federations.

Russia have been suspended from competing in IIHF events since the country invaded Ukraine in February 2022, but the Russian Ice Hockey Federation (RIHF) then successfully appealed that decision at Cas. The court said that IIHF arguments citing safety and security were "not supported by sufficient evidence", but the Hockey Federation of Ukraine said the ruling caused "special outrage".

The Canadian government has since informed its hockey authorities that it will not issue visas for Russians to play in next month's World Junior Championship, including those who currently play for teams in Canada, as long as the war continues. A number of countries had said they would refuse to play against Russia, if they were allowed to take part.

Despite the controversy, the return of Russia and Belarus to international sport has been gathering pace this year.

In March, several athletes from the two countries were allowed to compete under their national flags at the Winter Paralympics after partial suspensions by the International Paralympic Committee were lifted.

In July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) provisionally reinstated Russia to its competitions, stating a ban introduced in 2023 after the invasion of Ukraine was "no longer applicable".

However, sports federations can still enforce their own eligibility criteria. While World Gymnastics, World Aquatics and World Boxing have all removed restrictions on Russian athletes competing, a total ban has been maintained by World Athletics.

Last month, it was announced that Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships - the first time an Olympic federation has chosen to stage a global event in Russia since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Are we too reliant on big tech companies?

A critical Microsoft outage lasting more than 22 hours has raised questions about how heavily vital services rely on a handful of major tech firms.

The disruption, which affected Microsoft 365 services such as Outlook, was caused by routine automated checks that took some servers offline, overloading the remaining ones with traffic.

The recovery took nearly a full day while engineers gradually restored services, highlighting how embedded the tech giant's services are in modern society.

Flora Hamilton, executive director of the Small Business Charter, said the outage was a "stark reminder" of how much firms "rely on digital systems" - like Microsoft Outlook - "to keep their operations running".

"For many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), access to email is fundamental to everything from communicating with customers and suppliers to generating income," she said.

The disruption was not just confined to businesses, but also affected organisations and public institutions around the world.

Around 430 million people globally use Microsoft 365, and issues were reported across more than 70 countries.

The fallout from the outage had a wide-ranging effect , knocking out email systems for the US House of Representatives and Australian intelligence agencies, as well as disrupting court systems in Singapore and airline support desks in India.

Microsoft has since apologised for the issue, which it said was due to a technical failure rather than a cyber-attack.

There was no "ETA" for when services will be fully recovered, Microsoft added in a statement late on Friday (GMT).

Walter Pasquarelli, an AI strategist, told the BBC that for governments, businesses and critical infrastructure, the outage had "put their vulnerabilities and dependence in plain sight".

"Looking ahead, as AI assistants are plugged into our email, calendars and files, a failure like this may spread even further," he said.

Microsoft says email queues 'approaching normal levels' after global outage hits Outlook and Teams users

Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies, said while these kinds of outages weren't unheard of, what was unusual was the time it took for Microsoft to recover from it.

A spokesperson for the US tech company said "given the scale of demand" it restored services gradually.

"While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration," a spokesperson said.

Orosz said the resulting upset showed "our reliance on a few large US corporations".

He said a solution for the future could be to split services per region to reduce the impact, something which already happens with Amazon's cloud computing service, AWS.

For now, Microsoft said it was reviewing what went wrong, with the findings expected to inform steps to prevent a similar disruption from happening again.

Minisiteri y'ubuhinzi mu Rwanda ivuga ko ikibazo cy'ihindagurika ry'ibihe ari cyo cyabaye intandaro y'ibiciro bihanitse by'ibiribwa muri iki gihe.

Mu gihe abagana amasoko binubira ibiciro bikabije kuba hejuru, Minisitiri w'ubuhinzi Telesphore Ndabamenye avuga ko leta iri gushaka uko yakongera ibyanya byuhirwa (irrigation) kugira ngo abaturage bashobore guhinga no mu gihe cy'izuba.

Impungenge ku biciro by'ibiribwa zageze no mu nteko ishingamategeko, aho abadepite baherutse gusaba minisiteri y'ubuhinzi kugaragaza ingamba zirambye ifitiye ikibazo cy'ibiribwa.

Mu isoko rya Kimironko mu mujyi wa Kigali, ibiribwa bitandukanye ni byinshi ariko abaguzi bo baraza urusorongo.

Igiciro kiri hejuru ku bicuruzwa byinshi ni cyo gituma abaguzi atari benshi.

Muri iri soko ikilo cy'ibirayi kiragura hagati y'amafaranga 1100 na 1500.

Ni mu gihe mu isoko rya Musanze mu majyaruguru, hafatwa nk'ikigega cy'ibirayi, ho kigura hagati y'amafaranga 850 na 1000 kuri buri kilo.

Umubyeyi w'abana batatu yambwiye ko igiteye impungenge muri iki gihe ari uko ibiribwa byahenze muri rusange, mu gihe mu bihe byashize hashoboraga guhenda bimwe ariko ibindi bikaguma ku giciro cyoroheje.

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Yagize ati: "Wibaze ko n'ibijumba bigura amafaranga 1000 ku kilo, ubugari twiyambazaga na bwo igiciro cyarazamutse cyane kandi ibi ni bimwe mu biribwa twasigaranaga iyo ibindi byabaga byahenze.

"Ni ukurya rimwe ku munsi… saa sita cyangwa mu ijoro. Rwose hari inzara kandi iteye ubwoba."

Uruhande rw'abacuruzi na rwo rwemera ko ibiciro byazamutse cyane ariko na bo ngo baba babibonye bibahenze.

Umwe muri bo yagize ati: "Ibirayi ndabigurisha 1500 ku kilo. Birashoboka ko ari menshi bitewe n'ubushobozi bw'uje guhaha ariko natwe ni ko tuba twabibonye... Inzara iri hose, natwe abacuruzi itugeraho."

Ikigo cy'igihugu cy'ibarurishamibare kivuga ko ibiciro by'ibiribwa mu kwezi gushize kwa 10 byari byiyongereye ku rugero rungana na 19,5% ugereranyije n'uko ibintu byari bimeze igihe nk'iki umwaka ushize.

Imiterere y'ibiciro by'ibiribwa yateye impungenge kugera no mu nteko ishingamategeko, aho abadepite basaba ko hagira igikorwa byihutirwa.

Umwe mu badepite yagize ati: "Igishanga cya Nyabarongo gihingwamo ibisheke. Ariko se umusaruro wabyo ungana iki ugereranyije n'isukari igihugu gitumiza hanze? Niba iyo sukari atari nyinshi kuki ibi bishanga bitatangwa ngo bihingwemo ibindi nk'imboga, byadufasha no kugabanya ikibazo cy'imirire mibi?"

Hari n'abadepite basanga imikoreshereze mibi y'ubutaka buto igihugu gifite ishobora kugira ingaruka ku kibazo cy'ibiribwa muri rusange.

Uyu yagize ati: "Abaturage bahinga ikawa n'icyayi bemererwa kongera ubuso bw'ubutaka bahingaho nta cyo babanje gusabwa. Mu gihe byakomeza gutya aba bahinzi bagakomeza kongera ubutaka, byatuma tutabona aho duhinga ibihingwa ngandurarugo. Byazadutera inzara ikomeye."

Imbere y'abadepite, Minisitiri w'ubuhinzi Telesphore Ndabamenye na we yemeye ko ikibazo cy'ibiribwa kiriho koko kandi ko leta igerageza ibishoboka ngo kibonerwe umuti.

Yagize ati: "Imvura yatinze kugwa ituma umusaruro abantu bari bategereje ugabanuka cyane. Guverinoma irakora ibishoboka byose ngo yongere ubuso bw'ubutaka bwuhirwa [irrigation]. Turibaza ko umusaruro uvuye muri uku kuhira uzadufasha guhangana n'ibiciro by'ibiribwa."

Uretse kuba ubuhinzi bw'u Rwanda bushingira ku miterere y'ikirere kiba cyiza umusaruro ukaboneka, cyarakara inzara igatera, hari n'abasanga leta ikwiye kongera gukomorera abaturage bagahinga icyo bashaka, ndetse n'ibishanga bikomye bakemererwa kubibyaza umusaruro.

Ibi bikiyongeraho ubushakashatsi ku mbuto ibereye akarere runaka ndetse hakongerwa n'ubushobozi bw'ifumbire ikorerwa imbere mu gihugu.

The Metropolitan Police has launched an investigation into David Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences".

It comes after ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

The Met said that the allegations being investigated are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian, but as "part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences".

When those allegations were first reported, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

In a statement released on Friday, the Met said it had "received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s".

"Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers," the statement added.

Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney said: "We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened.

"We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process."

Allegations against the entertainer and children's author were published after he lost a legal bid to stop claims against him being made public by the media.

Some of the women in the investigation accused Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers.

One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.

He said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

The Guardian and ITV News said that several of the women, who do not know one another, allege they were targets of unwanted sexual advances from Walliams.

The investigation also claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another.

Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room.

In a letter addressed to journalists working on the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams wrote: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret.

"And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

Walliams shot to fame in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

Putin sounded uncompromising and confident at his talks with the US envoys

Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.

That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.

And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace?

The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."

Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.

What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.

The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 – the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.

Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.

What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia".

That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them.

But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow.

"In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week.

"Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement."

The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire".

"The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture."

Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table.

Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia.

This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US.

After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks.

But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken.

"Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.

At the talks with Witkoff and Kushner he was sounding uncompromising and confident.

The Americans are knocking at his door and seeking a deal and the Europeans are contemplating contacts with him. Last month the leaders of Norway and Finland reached out and called him.

And next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, Putin may have a separate meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Russian media are already comparing them to the "Big Three" - Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill - who met in 1945 to reorganise post-World War Two Europe.

And yet, after nearly five years of war, Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.

The Russian economy is under increasing pressure.

Ukrainian drone strikes continue to target Russian oil refineries, sparking fears of new fuel shortages.

But, so far, none of this has convinced the Kremlin leader to end the fighting.

Rochdale and York City meet for the first time since last season's dramatic title decider

It is just over six months since one of the greatest games to decide a title.

Rochdale and York City had clinched a huge 212 points between them heading into an extraordinary final-day showdown at Crown Oil Arena on 25 April.

In the end, York City clinched automatic promotion from the National League by the barest of margins, snatching a 1-1 draw courtesy of Josh Stones' stunning equaliser in the 13th minute of stoppage time.

Having ensured promotion in dramatic circumstances of their own through a tough play-off campaign, Rochdale joined them in League Two this term, with the pair facing each other for the first time since their epic fixture.

Plenty has changed for both clubs as they adapt to life back in the English Football League (EFL).

How are both clubs faring this season? And will they forever be linked by that historic day?

Josh Stones scored his 18th league goal of the season to secure the title for York

Saturday, 25 April 2026 will live long in the memory of not just both sets of supporters but neutrals as well, with fans across the world choosing to follow a fifth-tier football match on a busy day's action in late April.

The game came to life in the final stages. After York had spurned a fantastic opportunity to open the scoring late on through Stones, Rochdale fans inside the ground began to sense luck may be on their side.

Not least when Ian Henderson, Rochdale's cult hero, swung in a peach of a cross with the outside of his foot which was headed home at the far post by Emmanuel Dieseruvwe in the 95th minute.

Cue bedlam. Rochdale fans stormed the pitch in pure elation and emotion. They thought they were promoted.

"As a local radio commentator you want to capture what fans are feeling. As Emmanuel Dieseruvwe headed in on the 95th minute, myself and former Rochdale player Joe Bunney went big," BBC Radio Manchester commentator Alex Whitington said.

"It felt like that was the moment. We stood up to describe the pitch invasion and stayed standing to call Dale home."

But that gave the York players, and management staff, time to reset. More than six minutes passed between Rochdale's goal and York restarting the match. The visitors still believed.

In the 13th minute of stoppage time, Stones made no mistake with his second opportunity of the game, managing to squeeze the ball over the line following pinball in the penalty area - sending York up with virtually the final kick of the season.

"There was a split-second moment when then Rochdale boss Jimmy McNulty thought the referee had blown the whistle for full-time, only to find out that in fact the whistle meant his side were staying in the National League - momentarily," BBC Radio York's Dave Ward said.

Whitington added: "Stones' equaliser was bedlam. Not least because from our angle it wasn't clear if the ball had crossed the line.

"I cried 'oh no' four times. I think that encapsulates the emotion perfectly. I may never commentate on another ending like it."

Rochdale were forced into the play-offs where they eventually produced another comeback, this time against Boreham Wood at Wembley to seal their EFL return.

"The supporters can't wait to get back - they will love the banter. The rivalry between the fans will be brilliant and all those memories will come flooding back," Ward added.

York win promotion with 103rd-minute equaliser at Rochdale

Their day, until it wasn't - the title decider that had it all

National League champions York City decided to make the unusual move of swapping managers in the summer despite their last-gasp title win.

Stuart Maynard departed the club in July and was replaced by former Crawley boss Scott Lindsey the following day - a move met with anger by many supporters at the time.

After an unbeaten run of five league matches between September and October, Lindsey's reign in North Yorkshire is now beginning to take shape and the Minstermen are inside the play-off places despite losing their past two games.

Last season's National League top scorer Ollie Pearce has continued to bang the goals in since stepping up to the EFL for the first time.

Pearce has scored eight in all competitions this season, including inside 10 seconds in York's 4-0 thumping of Northampton Town last Saturday in the FA Cup. It was the competition's third-quickest goal of all time.

The 31-year-old striker has been ably supported by Alex Newby in the absence of Stones who has struggled with injuries this campaign.

Attacking midfielder Newby has six league goals so far this term, and the returning Stones did get his name on the scoresheet during the win against the Cobblers.

Looking to Saturday's match, Lindsey underlined the importance of using the psychological advantage last season's final-day showdown might provide.

"The importance is the players feel that environment when they turn up at the stadium again. They will have good memories, so we'll definitely be leaning on that," Lindsey told BBC Radio York.

"I may mention about the last time they were there. It can only be a good thing what happened there last time."

Incredible radio commentary of York City's promotion-sealing goal

Rochdale also changed their manager in the summer - although their hand was rather more forced.

McNulty made the short journey to Stockport County and in came former South Shields boss Ian Watson.

Dale had a tough start to life back in the EFL after three years away and Watson was given a vote of confidence by the board in early September to give him time to turn the club's fortunes around.

It had an immediate effect. Rochdale drew with Walsall and then went on to beat local rivals Oldham Athletic and Fleetwood Town in their next three matches - yet Rochdale welcome their opponents on the back of a five-game winless run.

Last season's 27-goal striker Dieseruvwe is yet to find the net in the league this term and Rochdale are 13 places below Saturday's opponents, however, just five points separate them in a tightly packed League Two table after 14 matches.

Ian Henderson, at 41 years old, is continuing to cast his spell on the EFL.

Into his second stint at Spotland, and 13th season as a Rochdale player, Henderson has scored twice in his past three league games despite not yet starting a match.

While York have loftier ambitions, 22nd place or higher in Rochdale's first season back in the fourth tier come close of play on 8 May would represent a successful return to the EFL.

If you’ve been on social media lately, chances are you’ve come across the conversations, memes and countless reactions surrounding the Microsoft outage.

From corporate professionals sharing their frustrations to people joking about being forced to remember how work was done before everything became digital, the internet has certainly had something to say about it.

And honestly, some of the reactions have been quite entertaining.

But having experienced a full working day of the disruption myself, I couldn’t help but think there was a much bigger conversation hiding behind all the jokes.

For many of us, Microsoft is practically part of our daily routine. Outlook is where our communication lives, Teams is where meetings happen, OneDrive is where documents are stored, and the wider Microsoft ecosystem has become deeply embedded in how organisations function.

So when these services suddenly become unavailable, even temporarily, the impact goes beyond not being able to send an email or join a meeting. It disrupts routines, interrupts communication and, in some cases, slows down entire operations.

Yesterday, some of us had to put aside the usual digital conveniences and find alternative, rather traditional ways of getting things done.

And guess what? The work still got done.

That, to me, was perhaps the most interesting part of the experience.

We have spent years embracing digital transformation, investing in systems and adopting tools that promise to make our organisations faster, smarter and more efficient. And rightly so. Technology has fundamentally changed the workplace for the better.

However, I think we sometimes overlook an important distinction: there is a difference between becoming more efficient through technology and becoming entirely dependent on it.

The outage was a timely reminder of that distinction.

What happens when the very systems that make our work easier suddenly become unavailable?

Can we still communicate? Can we access essential information? Can teams make decisions and keep operations moving? More importantly, do we have reliable alternatives, or have we built working environments that function only when everything is running perfectly?

These are questions worth asking, particularly for organisations that have invested heavily in digital transformation.

Perhaps the conversation should not only be about how quickly we can digitise our operations, but also about how resilient those operations are when the technology fails.

Digital transformation and business continuity should go hand in hand. Having alternative communication channels, accessible backups, documented processes and teams that know how to adapt should not be afterthoughts. They should be part of how we design our operations from the beginning.

And no, this is certainly not an argument for abandoning technology and returning to filing cabinets, handwritten reports and endless paperwork. Nobody is asking for that! 😂

But perhaps we should occasionally remind ourselves how to function without all the conveniences we have become accustomed to.

Because if there is one thing this experience has demonstrated, it is that even the most sophisticated digital environments are not immune to disruption.

Technology should enhance our ability to work, not become the only condition under which we can work.

Maybe one day, all this digital convenience will humble us again and send us back to the traditional ways of doing things. Perhaps the smartest thing we can do is stay prepared.

As for yesterday and today , we improvised, adapted, and got the work done.

The systems may have been down, but productivity did not have to be.

The writer Sylvie Sugira is Kigali Today Ltd’s Brand and Communications Consultant. She can be followed on Travel with Sy (@sylvie_sugira) – Instagram

Chris Van Hollen (L) says he will challenge Chuck Schumer (R) and that the Democrats need new leadership

US Senator Chuck Schumer is facing a challenge to his position as majority leader from his fellow Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, as the party prepares to take control of Congress after sweeping the midterm elections.

Van Hollen, 67, said in a post on X on Thursday that Americans had voted for change earlier this month and "to deliver, we need new leadership".

Schumer, 75, has led Democrats in the chamber since 2017, serving as both majority and minority leader. He was first elected to the Senate in 1999.

Following the midterms earlier this month, his position has come under pressure by some left-wing Democrats who see him as too moderate and part of the party establishment.

Responding to the challenge, Schumer, who represents New York, said he welcomed "any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead".

He added that he was "proud of what we've accomplished together" in the midterms and that he had "the votes to continue as Democratic leader".

A vote on the new Senate leader will be held behind closed doors in early December and the winner will assume the role on 4 January, when Democrats take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives after their midterms successes.

The move by Van Hollen, who represents Maryland, marks the most significant step by a high-profile Democrat to challenge the party's existing leadership following last week's midterms victory.

He wrote that Americans had called on the party to "unrig an economy rigged against working people" in an X post announcing his plan to run.

"We should not be preserving our institutions if they are not delivering for the American people," he said at a summit in Colorado hosted by majority Democrats. "And we should be making delivering for the American people the single mission of our government, even when that means shaking things up."

He added: "This country does not belong to the people who can afford to buy influence. It belongs to all of us. And it's time we govern like that."

In recent years, Van Hollen has taken positions popular with those on the left of his party.

In 2024, he supported restricting weapons shipments to Israel and criticised the Biden administration over its role in the war in Gaza.

Van Hollen - who has served in the Senate for nearly a decade - acknowledged that he was an "underdog" in an interview with MS NOW, but added that he believed the race was "very much in flux".

Independent Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed have both publicly come out in support of Van Hollen - while others have also called for new leadership.

Sanders said he believed Van Hollen "will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families".

El-Sayed said the challenger would bring "bold leadership" and lead with both "courage and experience".

Others Democrats have publicly backed Schumer.

Senator Jacky Rosen of Nevada said: "He has the experience and the fight to continue leading our diverse caucus at this crucial moment."

Senator Kirsten Gillibrand said: "You will see, despite all the grumblings, enormous gratitude for the hard work he has done to get us to this position."

In future, German spies working for the BND foreign intelligence service will be able to conduct covert operations abroad

Germany's foreign and domestic intelligence services are to be given greater powers to combat espionage, terrorism and sabotage after the country's parliament, the Bundestag, approved a major overhaul of its legislation.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, who championed the bill, has called it a "reform of the century", necessary because of the increasing threats from foreign powers.

But the Left Party's security spokeswoman, Clara Bünger, said Dobrindt was creating a new German secret police.

The legislation gives numerous new powers to Germany's BND federal intelligence service, and its BfV domestic service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution.

In the Bundestag, 309 MPs voted in favour of the new law on intelligence services, while 190 voted against and 71 abstained.

For historical reasons, German intelligence has mainly focused on gathering information rather than acting on it.

In future, German spies working for the BND, which is responsible for foreign intelligence, will be able to conduct covert operations abroad, including sabotage.

This could include paralysing the servers of state-sponsored hacker groups, disrupting disinformation networks, or even disrupting supply chains for weapons.

Agents for the domestic intelligence service, the BfV, will no longer to be limited to gathering information. For the first time they will be able to take protective action against property and IT systems, if specific threats are identified.

That means they will be allowed to dismantle or break explosives or weapons, divert or block data flows during cyber-attacks, delete or falsify data stored for malicious purposes, and plant false information on those involved.

Under certain conditions, BfV agents will also be permitted to enter homes covertly. However, the measure must always be authorised in advance.

They will also be given wider powers of digital surveillance, including monitoring encrypted telecommunications and carrying out online searches. They will also be allowed to use AI-supported data analysis and biometric image matching on the internet.

The government says the reform is needed because of an increase in foreign espionage, particularly from Russia, China and Iran.

"We are the target of hybrid threats," said Dobrindt. "Germany is a theatre of operations for terrorism, extremism and foreign powers."

In August, a drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig Airport, close to Ukrainian cargo planes. However, it failed to explode as the bomb's detonator was apparently faulty.

German authorities say Russia was behind the attack.

The new law has been bitterly criticised by some opposition politicians, even though Dobrindt has said it is "madness" to think it means that Germany is creating a new secret police.

And Clara Bünger from the Left Party told public broadcaster ARD that the new law was "a monster… summoning ghosts that we will probably never be able to get rid of".

The separation between the police and the secret service, she warned, was "being eroded" - and Bünger said that had been a lesson learned from the Nazi era.

"This means the secret service is being granted executive powers and will not only be allowed to act pre-emptively, but will also be granted police powers."

However, Sonja Eichwede of the centre-left SPD, which is part of Germany's governing coalition, said the reforms would make a significant contribution to ensuring the country's democracy was "robust and resilient".

Businesses in Nyagatare are exploring how to raise long-term financing through Rwanda’s capital market, including by issuing shares or corporate bonds.

A meeting held this morning brought together the Capital Market Authority, the Private Sector Federation, Rwanda Stock Exchange, Rwanda National Investment Trust, BK Capital and other market partners.

They presented financing options for businesses seeking to expand and discussed how companies can prepare to attract investors.

The session is part of the 2026 Capital Markets Roadshows, running from October 27 to November 25. The programme offers guidance on corporate governance, financial reporting and business readiness.

Companies seeking investment need clear strategies, reliable financial records and sound governance to demonstrate their credibility to potential investors.

Businesses can raise money by selling shares, giving investors part ownership, or by issuing corporate bonds and repaying investors under agreed terms.

Small and medium-sized enterprises can also consider the Rwanda Stock Exchange’s SME Market Segment, which has lower entry thresholds than the main market and offers access to licensed advisers.

The roadshow comes as Rwanda’s capital market continues to expand. In the 2024/25 financial year, three corporate bond issuances worth Rwf 46 billion were approved.

Market capitalisation on the Rwanda Stock Exchange rose 3.4% to Rwf 3.84 trillion, while assets managed by collective investment schemes grew 12% to Rwf 71.4 billion.
